# The hybrid breeding programme, and the population genetics it rests on {#sec-hybrid-programme}



The preface states the optimisation problem. This chapter states what that
problem is a part of. Its first half follows a hybrid programme through one
cycle, names the four stages the rest of the book refers to, and marks where in
that cycle diversity is lost. Its second half gives the population genetics the
later chapters assume: allele frequency, Hardy-Weinberg proportions, gene
diversity, identity by descent and by state, coancestry, the inbreeding
coefficient and its namesakes, drift and effective size. Each is defined once,
with the identity that later chapters lean on checked numerically. Derivations
stay in the chapters that use them; this one points to them.

The programme described is the one whose assumptions @sec-era-programme declares
as A1--A8. The examples below use four of them, restated here because they are
used before that section is reached:

- two heterotic pools, A and B, maintained as closed breeding units, whose single
  crosses are the product (A1);
- parent lines fully inbred, by doubled-haploid (DH) induction or by selfing to
  fixation (A2);
- germplasm recycled only within its own pool (A3);
- markers neutral and biallelic, coded $0/0.5/1$ as the within-individual
  frequency $x_{ik}$ of the reference allele, as in @eq-x-freq (A5).

The live examples run at the teaching scale of `_common.R`:
25 + 25 lines,
2000 markers, every A $\times$ B single cross formed, pool frequencies drawn by
the Balding-Nichols model of @sec-simulating-crosses.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ctx  <- simulate_data(book_cfg)                 # hybrids: X, f; lines: fL
GL   <- simulate_lines(book_cfg) / 2            # the same lines, coded 0/1
pool <- ctx[["pool"]]
fL   <- ctx[["fL"]]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fL, molecular_coancestry(GL))))
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
c(lines_A = sum(pool == "A"), lines_B = sum(pool == "B"),
  hybrids = ctx[["N"]], markers = ctx[["m"]])
#> lines_A lines_B hybrids markers 
#>      25      25     625    2000
```
:::


## The programme, end to end {#sec-hp-cycle}

**Heterotic pools.** A hybrid programme maintains two (sometimes more) sets of
lines, the heterotic pools or groups, and makes its product by crossing a line of
one pool with a line of the other. Lines are not crossed within a pool to make a
product; within a pool they are crossed only to make new lines. The pools are
kept apart because the value of an A $\times$ B single cross depends on the
complementarity of the two parents, and that complementarity depends on the two
pools' allele frequencies differing (@sec-heterosis). How lines come to be
assigned to a pool is itself an unsettled empirical question
(@sec-plant-literature); this book takes the assignment as given.

**Inbred parent lines.** The parents are homozygous lines. Selfing from a
non-inbred plant ($F_0 = 0$) raises the inbreeding coefficient as
$1 - F_t = (1/2)^t$, because each generation of selfing halves the probability
that the two alleles at a locus are not identical by descent
[@falconer1996, ch. 5]; after six generations
$F_6 = 0.9844$. A doubled haploid reaches $F = 1$ in one step: it
is a single gamete with its chromosome set doubled. Either route delivers a line
with no heterozygous locus, and that fact carries much of the algebra of the
book.

**The product: the F1 single cross.** Because both parents are homozygous, the
genotype of the F1 between lines $a$ and $b$ is determined without sampling: at
each locus it carries one allele from each parent, and it is heterozygous exactly
where the two parents differ (@eq-hybrid-dosage). Seed of the same single cross
produced in two seasons is genetically the same hybrid. The commercial product
carries heterozygosity; neither parent does.

**Testing in cross, and combining ability.** A line is not worth what it yields
on its own; it is worth what its hybrids yield. Lines are therefore evaluated in
cross with lines of the opposite pool -- either against one or a few fixed
**testers** (a testcross, @sec-mating-tester) or in a sparse factorial among the
candidates of both pools (@sec-mating-sparse). The cross means are read through
the partition into general and specific combining ability defined by
@sprague1942, written as a linear model for a factorial between two sets of
lines (the North Carolina Design II of @comstock1948; the notation $g$, $s$ is
that of @griffing1956),

$$
\bar y_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij} + \bar e_{ij},
$$ {#eq-hp-gca-sca}

with $\bar y_{ij}$ the mean of hybrid $i \times j$ over its plots, $\mu$ the mean
of the reference set of crosses, $g^A_i$ the general combining ability (GCA) of
pool-A line $i$ (what it carries into every cross it enters), $g^B_j$ that of
pool-B line $j$, $s_{ij}$ the specific combining ability (SCA) of the pair (what
depends on which two lines met), and $\bar e_{ij}$ the plot error of the mean.
@eq-hp-gca-sca is the model of @sec-mating-estimation, where its estimation is
treated.

Both effects are defined **relative to a reference set of crosses**, and so
against a tester pool. @sec-mating-estimation writes the GCA of a pool-A line as
$\sum_k [a_k + d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})]\,\delta u_{ik}$, and @sec-heterosis-gca-sca
derives its dominance part $\sum_k d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})\,\delta u_{ik}$: an average effect of
substitution evaluated at **pool B's** frequencies $p_{Bk}$, with $a_k$ and $d_k$
the additive effect and the dominance deviation at locus $k$ and
$\delta u_{ik}$ line $i$'s centred 0/1 genotype. Without dominance
($d_k \equiv 0$) the GCA of a line is the same against every tester set; with
dominance it moves with the testers' frequencies. The chunk below takes the
dominance part alone, on the book data with a gamma-distributed $d_k$ (the
draw @sec-heterosis uses; an illustrative assumption, not an estimate), and
computes the GCA of the same 25 pool-A lines against two
disjoint halves of pool B.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
U <- GL[pool == "A", ]; V <- GL[pool == "B", ]
set.seed(4)
d <- rgamma(ncol(GL), 2, 4)                      # dominance deviations, d_k > 0
half <- seq_len(nrow(V)) <= nrow(V) / 2
g1 <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V[half, ],  d)[["gca_A"]]
g2 <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V[!half, ], d)[["gca_A"]]
# GCA is the row effect of the complete factorial against those testers
H1 <- outer(drop(U %*% d), drop(V[half, ] %*% d), "+") - 2 * U %*% (d * t(V[half, ]))
gca_err <- max(abs(g1 - (rowMeans(H1) - mean(H1))))
stopifnot(gca_err < 1e-10)
gca_cor  <- cor(g1, g2)
top5_shr <- length(intersect(order(-g1)[seq_len(5)], order(-g2)[seq_len(5)]))
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
c(correlation = gca_cor, top5_shared = top5_shr)
#> correlation top5_shared 
#>   0.8587374   3.0000000
```
:::


Result. Against the first half of pool B (12 lines; the second has
13) the GCA equals the row effect of the factorial to within
4\times 10^{-13}; the correlation between the dominance parts of
the GCA computed against the two halves is 0.859, and
3 of the five best lines are the same. Interpretation. Under
dominance, the same line, with the same genotype, has a different general
combining ability against a different tester set: GCA is then a property of a
line against a tester pool, not of the line alone; with $d_k \equiv 0$ it would
not depend on the testers. The size of the disagreement here belongs to the
dominance part alone ($a_k \equiv 0$), one dominance draw, one seed and testers
of 12 and 13 lines, and is not a general estimate. The additive part
$\sum_k a_k\,\delta u_{ik}$ is the same against both halves; with additive
effects independent of the dominance deviations, adding it pulls the
correlation towards 1, so the case shown is the one that maximises the
disagreement.

**The four stages.** @sec-stages divides a cycle of the programme into four
stages and measures diversity at each. The names, listed in @tbl-hp-stages, are
used throughout the book.

| Stage | What is selected | Where the book treats it |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | conserving the heterotic groups (pool level) | @sec-subdivided, @sec-stages |
| **S2** | choosing parents and crosses for DH induction | @sec-sizing, @sec-stages |
| **S3** | selecting lines per se | @sec-stages |
| **S4** | hybrid mining | @sec-collapse, @sec-ocs, @sec-combinatorial |

: The four stages of a cycle of a hybrid programme, what is selected at each, and the chapters of this book that treat it. {#tbl-hp-stages}

The selection problem stated in the preface -- choose $n_{sel}$ of $N$ candidate
hybrids under a diversity budget $\alpha_{\max}$ -- is S4. Testing in cross
(@eq-hp-gca-sca) supplies the predicted values that S4 selects on; which crosses
are grown and where is the subject of the Mating and testing design part.

**Recycling.** The lines that prove themselves in cross are intercrossed
**within their own pool** to start the next cycle, and new DH lines are derived
from those within-pool crosses. Selection information crosses the pool boundary;
germplasm does not. A DH derived from an A $\times$ B hybrid would carry both
pools' alleles and erode the divergence the product depends on (assumption A3 of
@sec-era-programme). This is reciprocal recurrent selection [@comstock1949],
and `run_cycles()` in @sec-cycles implements it. @fig-hp-cycle draws one cycle.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)); plot.new(); plot.window(c(0, 100), c(0, 64))
box_ <- function(x, y, w, h, lab, col) {
  rect(x, y, x + w, y + h, col = adjustcolor(col, 0.18), border = col)
  text(x + w / 2, y + h / 2, lab, cex = 0.62, col = book_pal[["ink"]])
}
arr  <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, ...) arrows(x0, y0, x1, y1, length = 0.06, lwd = 1.4, ...)
loss <- function(x, y) points(x, y, pch = 25, cex = 0.9,
                              bg = book_pal[["loss"]], col = book_pal[["loss"]])
for (g in c("A", "B")) {
  y  <- if (g == "A") 44 else 8
  cl <- book_pal[[g]]
  box_(1,  y, 17, 12, paste0("S1\npool ", g, "\ninbred lines"), cl)
  box_(23, y, 19, 12, paste0("S2\ncrosses within ", g, "\n-> DH lines"), cl)
  box_(47, y, 15, 12, "S3\nlines\nper se", cl)
  arr(18, y + 6, 23, y + 6, col = cl); arr(42, y + 6, 47, y + 6, col = cl)
  arr(62, y + 6, 67, if (g == "A") 36 else 28, col = cl)
  loss(32.5, y + 13.8); loss(54.5, y + 13.8)
}
box_(67, 24, 13, 16, "A x B crosses\nin trials:\ntestcross or\nfactorial\n(GCA, SCA)",
     book_pal[["mid"]])
box_(85, 24, 14, 16, "S4\nhybrid\nmining:\nselect single\ncrosses", book_pal[["mid"]])
arr(80, 32, 85, 32, col = book_pal[["mid"]]); loss(92, 41.8)
arr(92, 24, 92, 22, col = book_pal[["ink"]])
text(92, 20.5, "commercial F1", cex = 0.62, font = 2)
# recycling, within pool only
# dashed shafts; the heads are drawn solid, since arrows() dashes the head too
segments(c(73.5, 73.5, 9.5), c(40, 61, 61), c(73.5, 9.5, 9.5), c(61, 61, 57.2),
         lty = 2, lwd = 1.4, col = book_pal[["A"]])
arr(9.5, 57.2, 9.5, 56, col = book_pal[["A"]])
segments(c(73.5, 73.5, 9.5), c(24, 3, 3), c(73.5, 9.5, 9.5), c(3, 3, 6.8),

arr(9.5, 6.8, 9.5, 8, col = book_pal[["B"]])
```

**Where diversity is lost.** Every step marked in @fig-hp-cycle samples or
selects a subset of $n_{sel}$ of the $N$ members of a pool. A subset never
carries an allele its pool lacks, so the number of alleles can stay the same or
fall, never rise. Gene diversity behaves differently. A subset drawn *at
random* has an expected group coancestry $\theta_S$ (the mean of all pairwise
coancestries in the set, diagonal included; defined in @sec-hp-popgen) larger
than the pool's by $(1/n_{sel} - 1/N)(\bar f_d - \bar f_o)$, with $\bar f_d$
the pool's mean self-coancestry and $\bar f_o$ its mean coancestry between
distinct members, so its expected gene diversity $GD_S = 1 - \theta_S$
(@eq-hp-gd) is lower by the same amount (@sec-baseline). A
subset *selected* on some criterion carries no such guarantee, and one selected
for diversity can exceed its pool. The chunk below measures both on the book's
hybrids, with the diversity-only greedy `sel_greedy(w = 0)` as the selected
subset.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_sub   <- 20
gd_pool <- gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx[["N"]]), ctx)
fd <- mean(diag(ctx[["f"]])); fo <- mean(ctx[["f"]][upper.tri(ctx[["f"]])])
set.seed(5)
gd_rnd  <- replicate(200, gene_diversity(sample.int(ctx[["N"]], n_sub), ctx))
gd_div  <- gene_diversity(sel_greedy(ctx, n_sub, w = 0), ctx)
sub_gd  <- c(pool = gd_pool, random_mean = mean(gd_rnd),
             random_se = sd(gd_rnd) / sqrt(length(gd_rnd)),
             random_expected = gd_pool - (1 / n_sub - 1 / ctx[["N"]]) * (fd - fo),
             random_max = max(gd_rnd), diversity_greedy = gd_div)
stopifnot(abs(sub_gd[["random_mean"]] - sub_gd[["random_expected"]]) <
            3 * sub_gd[["random_se"]],
          sub_gd[["diversity_greedy"]] > sub_gd[["pool"]])
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
fmt(sub_gd, 4)
#>             pool      random_mean        random_se  random_expected 
#>           0.3281           0.3209           0.0001           0.3210 
#>       random_max diversity_greedy 
#>           0.3251           0.3296
```
:::


Result. The 625 hybrids have $GD$ = 0.3281;
200 random subsets of 20 average 0.3209
(s.e. 10^{-4}, expected
0.321), the largest of them
0.3251; the 20 hybrids chosen for diversity
alone have 0.3296, above the pool.
Interpretation. A loss of gene diversity at a step of @fig-hp-cycle is
guaranteed only in expectation and only for sampling; selection can move a
subset either way, and the comparison that isolates what selection did is
against random subsets of the same size, not against the pool. That is why the
diversity loss $\alpha = (GD_{\text{ref}} - GD_S)/GD_{\text{ref}}$, the quantity
the budget $\alpha_{\max}$ bounds, is measured against $GD_{\text{ref}}$, the
gene diversity of a random subset of the same size (@sec-baseline). The
numbers belong to one pool pair, one subset size and one seed.

At S2 a few crosses are chosen among
all within-pool pairs and each DH line is one gamete of its cross; at S3 and S4
lines and hybrids are truncated on merit; at recycling the next cycle is founded
by the few lines that won in cross. In the end-to-end simulation of
@sec-stages, the largest share of the loss falls at S2, not at S4 where
optimisation effort usually goes; that result is the simulation's, at its
scale, and is reported there with its conditions. Between the pools the
movement is the opposite: within-pool selection and drift push the two pools'
frequencies apart, so between-pool divergence tends to grow while within-pool
diversity falls (@sec-subdivided). Both trends are reported from genotyped
germplasm: between Stiff Stalk and Non-Stiff Stalk lines over forty years of a
private European dent maize programme, with within-group diversity declining
[@kadoumi2025], and as increasing differentiation between breeding pools across
the history of North American maize lines [@vanheerwaarden2012]; the second
attributes little of the genome-wide pattern to selection. @sec-plant-literature
places these results among the rest of the plant literature. A single pool-wide statistic sees the sum of two
quantities moving in opposite directions, which is why the book partitions it.

## The population genetics the book assumes {#sec-hp-popgen}

Symbols follow @sec-notation. $p_k$ is the frequency of the reference allele at
marker $k$ in a stated set of individuals, $q_k = 1 - p_k$; $p_{Ak}$, $p_{Bk}$
are the frequencies among the lines of pool A and pool B, $\bar p_k$ a group
mean, and $p_{0,k}$ the frozen base frequency of the founding candidate pool.

### Allele frequency and Hardy-Weinberg proportions

For a set of $n$ individuals with within-individual frequencies $x_{ik}$, the
allele frequency at marker $k$ is $\bar p_k = n^{-1}\sum_i x_{ik}$: every
individual contributes equally, and a homozygous line contributes one allele
identity counted twice. In a large population with random union of gametes and
no selection, migration or mutation, one generation of random mating sets the
genotype frequencies to $p^2$, $2pq$ and $q^2$, the Hardy-Weinberg proportions
[@falconer1996, ch. 1]. Neither of the two sets a hybrid programme measures is in
those proportions. A pool of inbred lines has genotype frequencies $p$, $0$, $q$;
a set of A $\times$ B single crosses has every allele from pool A paired with one
from pool B, never with another from A. Hardy-Weinberg is used in this book as a
reference, the heterozygosity a set *would* have under random union of its
gametes, not as a description of any set in it.

### Gene diversity, expected and observed heterozygosity

The expected heterozygosity of a set is that Hardy-Weinberg reference, averaged
over loci, and with $\theta_S$ the group coancestry of set $S$ (the mean of the
coancestry submatrix, diagonal included; defined below) it is exactly gene
diversity:

$$
GD_S \;=\; 1 - \theta_S \;=\; \frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m} 2\,\bar p_k \bar q_k \;=\; H_e .
$$ {#eq-hp-gd}

$m$ is the number of markers and $\bar p_k$ the frequency in $S$. $H_e$ is Nei's
gene diversity [@nei1973] in its plug-in form, without the small-sample
correction, on the base of the set's own frequencies; @sec-identity derives the
identity. Observed heterozygosity $H_o$ is the fraction of heterozygous loci
actually present, averaged over the individuals of the set. The two coincide in
expectation only under Hardy-Weinberg proportions, and the hybrid programme
violates them in both directions:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pA <- colMeans(GL[pool == "A", ]); pB <- colMeans(GL[pool == "B", ])
all_h <- seq_len(ctx[["N"]])
gp    <- gd_partition(all_h, ctx)
het <- c(Ho_lines  = mean(GL == 0.5),
         He_pool_A = mean(2 * pA * (1 - pA)),
         Ho_hybrid = mean(ctx[["X"]] == 0.5),
         He_hybrid = he_nei(all_h, ctx),
         GD_hybrid = gene_diversity(all_h, ctx))
stopifnot(het[["Ho_lines"]] == 0,   # coding guard: GL is 0/1 by construction (A2)
          isTRUE(all.equal(het[["He_pool_A"]], 1 - mean(fL[pool == "A", pool == "A"]))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(het[["GD_hybrid"]], het[["He_hybrid"]])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(het[["He_hybrid"]], gp[["GD_T"]])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(het[["Ho_hybrid"]], gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]])))
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
fmt(het, 4)
#>  Ho_lines He_pool_A Ho_hybrid He_hybrid GD_hybrid 
#>    0.0000    0.2953    0.3617    0.3281    0.3281
```
:::


Result. The lines are heterozygous at no locus, by construction (A2: they are
coded 0/1; the assertion guards the coding, it measures nothing), while pool A's expected
heterozygosity is 0.295, equal to one minus pool A's
group coancestry. Over all 625 hybrids, $1 - \theta_S$ equals $H_e$
(@eq-hp-gd), and the observed heterozygosity 0.362
exceeds the expected 0.328 by exactly
$GD_{BS}$ = 0.0336, the between-pool term of the partition of
@sec-subdivided. Interpretation. In inbred lines observed heterozygosity is a
purity check and carries no information on diversity; in the hybrids it exceeds
the Hardy-Weinberg reference by the divergence between the pools. That excess
is the identity $H_o = GD_T + GD_{BS}$ derived in @sec-heterosis-identity, which
holds for the complete factorial; the decomposition is exact, the magnitudes are
those of one simulated pool pair.

### Identity by descent, identity by state, coancestry

Two alleles are **identical by descent** (IBD) if both are copies of one allele
in a defined base population; they are **identical in state** (IBS) if they are
the same allele, whatever their origin. IBD is defined only relative to a base:
change the base and the probabilities change. Markers observe state, not
descent.

The **coancestry** $f_{ij}$ of individuals $i$ and $j$ is the probability that
an allele drawn at random from $i$ and one drawn at random from $j$, at the same
locus, are IBD [@malecot1948]; the inbreeding coefficient of a progeny of
$i \times j$ equals the coancestry of its parents [@falconer1996, ch. 5].
Replacing IBD by IBS gives the molecular coancestry of @eq-f-molecular, the
matrix $\mathbf{f}$ every diversity metric in the book is computed on
[@caballero2002]. The two are related. Let the alleles that are not IBD be
independent draws from the base frequencies $p_{0,k}$ (no mutation, neutral
loci, the pedigree coancestry computed relative to that base), and write the
pedigree coancestry as $A_{ij}/2$, half the pedigree relationship. Then two
alleles are IBS either because they are IBD or, failing that, by chance, and in
expectation over Mendelian sampling and loci

$$
\mathbb{E}[f_{ij}] \;=\; \frac{A_{ij}}{2} \;+\; \Big(1 - \frac{A_{ij}}{2}\Big)\,
\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\big(p_{0,k}^2 + q_{0,k}^2\big),
$$ {#eq-hp-ibs-ibd}

the form @eding2001 use to estimate kinship from marker similarity. The chunk
checks @eq-hp-ibs-ibd on full sibs ($A_{ij}/2 = 1/4$) and on unrelated
individuals ($A_{ij} = 0$): each replicate draws two parents in Hardy-Weinberg
proportions from a base with uniform $p_{0,k}$, breeds two full sibs from them,
and uses the two parents themselves as the unrelated pair, at unlinked loci.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_ibs <- 2000; n_pair <- 200; p0_lim <- c(0.05, 0.95)
set.seed(21)
p0 <- runif(m_ibs, p0_lim[1], p0_lim[2])
ibs_base <- mean(p0^2 + (1 - p0)^2)
dip <- function() (rbinom(m_ibs, 1, p0) + rbinom(m_ibs, 1, p0)) / 2   # 0/0.5/1
gam <- function(g) ifelse(g == 0.5, rbinom(m_ibs, 1, 0.5), g)        # one gamete
f_fs <- f_un <- numeric(n_pair)
for (r in seq_len(n_pair)) {
  mo <- dip(); fa <- dip()
  o1 <- (gam(mo) + gam(fa)) / 2; o2 <- (gam(mo) + gam(fa)) / 2
  f_fs[r] <- molecular_coancestry(rbind(o1, o2))[1, 2]
  f_un[r] <- molecular_coancestry(rbind(mo, fa))[1, 2]
}
ibs <- c(full_sib = mean(f_fs), full_sib_se = sd(f_fs) / sqrt(n_pair),
         full_sib_expected = 1/4 + 3/4 * ibs_base,
         unrelated = mean(f_un), unrelated_se = sd(f_un) / sqrt(n_pair),
         unrelated_expected = ibs_base)
stopifnot(abs(ibs[["full_sib"]] - ibs[["full_sib_expected"]]) < 3 * ibs[["full_sib_se"]],
          abs(ibs[["unrelated"]] - ibs[["unrelated_expected"]]) < 3 * ibs[["unrelated_se"]])
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
fmt(ibs, 4)
#>           full_sib        full_sib_se  full_sib_expected          unrelated 
#>             0.7264             0.0004             0.7264             0.6351 
#>       unrelated_se unrelated_expected 
#>             0.0004             0.6352
```
:::


Result. Over 200 replicates, 2000 loci and
$p_{0,k} \sim U(0.05, 0.95)$, the mean molecular coancestry of
full sibs is
0.7264 (s.e. 4\times 10^{-4}) against
0.7264 from @eq-hp-ibs-ibd, and that of
unrelated pairs 0.6351 against
0.6352. Interpretation. Rearranged, @eq-hp-ibs-ibd
says that molecular coancestry is the floor
$m^{-1}\sum_k (p_{0,k}^2 + q_{0,k}^2)$ set by the base frequencies plus the
pedigree coancestry $A_{ij}/2$ scaled by one minus that floor, not plus the
pedigree coancestry itself. Full sibs are therefore expected to exceed unrelated
pairs by one quarter of one minus the floor,
0.0912, not by
$1/4$, and unrelated individuals do not have $f_{ij} = 0$ but $f_{ij}$ near the
floor. That is why $\mathbf{f}$ is read as a
comparison between sets measured on the same markers, and why it is never
centred to make that floor vanish (@sec-why-not-g). The agreement is a Monte
Carlo one, under unlinked loci and a known base, from one seed.

The diagonal of $\mathbf{f}$ is the **self-coancestry** $s_i = f_{ii}$, the
probability that two alleles drawn with replacement from $i$ are identical:
$s_i = (1 + F_i)/2$, which is 1 for an inbred line and 0.5 for an individual
heterozygous at every marker (@sec-f-molecular). **Group coancestry** $\theta_S$
is the mean of all $f_{ij}$ over pairs in $S$, the diagonal included
[@cockerham1967]; including the diagonal is what makes @eq-hp-gd exact.

### The inbreeding coefficient, and three quantities that share its letter

The **inbreeding coefficient** $F_i$ of an individual is the probability that
its two alleles at a locus are IBD, the definition of @malecot1948; @wright1922
introduced it as the correlation between uniting gametes. Its molecular
counterpart in this book is the fraction of markers at which $i$ is homozygous.
For a single cross the molecular $F_i$ is exactly the molecular coancestry of its
two parent lines, $F_{(ab)} = f^L_{ab}$, because two homozygous lines agree in
state exactly where their F1 is homozygous:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
F_hyb <- rowMeans(ctx[["X"]] != 0.5)
ped   <- ctx[["ped"]]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(F_hyb, fL[cbind(ped[["a"]], ped[["b"]])])))
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
c(max_abs_diff = max(abs(F_hyb - fL[cbind(ped[["a"]], ped[["b"]])])))
#> max_abs_diff 
#>            0
```
:::


With inbred parents, individual $F$ carries no management information: it is 1
for every line by construction (A2 of @sec-era-programme), and for a hybrid it
is a property of the pair of parents, already in $\mathbf{f}^L$. Three other
quantities share the letter and are not the same thing:

- $F_{drift}$ (@sec-genomic-era) is a property of a pool *through time*: the
  standardised squared change of allele frequencies from the frozen base
  $p_{0,k}$, averaged over markers [@meuwissen2020]. It is never negative.
  $F_{hom}$, its homozygosity-lens companion, is the proportional loss of
  heterozygosity against the same base and can be negative.
- $F_{ST}$ is a property of a set of subpopulations *at one time*: in this book
  $GD_{BS}/GD_T$, the between-pool share of gene diversity
  (@sec-subdivided, after @wright1951 and @nei1973).
- $F_{BN}$, `fst` in the code, is the Balding-Nichols parameter with which the
  simulations draw the two pools' frequencies [@balding1995]. It is a setting of
  the simulation, not a statistic computed on it, and @sec-notation shows that
  the two differ.

### Drift and effective size

In a finite population, the allele copies passed to the next generation are a
sample of those present, so allele frequencies change by chance alone. This is
**drift**. Let $n_{gam}$ be the number of allele copies sampled per generation,
with no selection, mutation or migration. Then expected heterozygosity decays
geometrically,

$$
\mathbb{E}[H_t] \;=\; H_0\Big(1 - \frac{1}{n_{gam}}\Big)^{t},
\qquad \Delta F = \frac{1}{n_{gam}},
\qquad N_e = \frac{1}{2\Delta F},
$$ {#eq-hp-drift}

with $H_t$ the expected heterozygosity at generation $t$, $\Delta F$ the
per-generation rate of inbreeding, and $N_e$ the **effective size**: the number
of individuals of an idealised random-mating diploid population, which passes
$n_{gam} = 2N_e$ copies, that would drift at the same rate
[@falconer1996, ch. 3--4]. In a hybrid programme the sampling unit matters by a
factor of two. A crossing block of $n$ plants intermated at random passes $2n$
allele copies per locus ($N_e = n$); a pool re-derived as $n$ DH lines passes
$n$, one per line ($N_e = n/2$), because a homozygous line contributes a single
allele identity (@sec-era-step4). The chunk checks both against
@eq-hp-drift, with every locus starting at $p = 0.5$ and each independent locus treated as a replicate.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_dr <- 20000; t_gen <- 10; n_plants <- 10
drift_ratio <- function(n_gam) {               # H_t / H_0 per locus
  p <- rep(0.5, m_dr)
  for (t in seq_len(t_gen)) p <- rbinom(m_dr, n_gam, p) / n_gam
  2 * p * (1 - p) / 0.5
}
set.seed(11); r_cb <- drift_ratio(2 * n_plants)   # crossing block of 10 plants
set.seed(12); r_dh <- drift_ratio(n_plants)       # pool re-derived as 10 DH lines
dr <- rbind(crossing_block = c(simulated = mean(r_cb), se = sd(r_cb) / sqrt(m_dr),
                               expected = (1 - 1 / (2 * n_plants))^t_gen),
            DH_pool        = c(simulated = mean(r_dh), se = sd(r_dh) / sqrt(m_dr),
                               expected = (1 - 1 / n_plants)^t_gen))
stopifnot(all(abs(dr[, "simulated"] - dr[, "expected"]) < 3 * dr[, "se"]))
# verification echo: the text reports these values; not a results table
fmt(dr, 4)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|               | simulated|     se| expected|
|:--------------|---------:|------:|--------:|
|crossing_block |    0.5997| 0.0026|   0.5987|
|DH_pool        |    0.3496| 0.0029|   0.3487|

:::
:::


Result. Over 20,000 loci, after 10 generations
with 10 parents, the crossing block
retains 0.6 of its heterozygosity
(expected 0.599) and the DH pool
0.35 (expected
0.349), each within three standard errors.
Interpretation. Under neutrality the same number of parents drifts twice as fast
when the next generation is a set of DH lines. Selection makes the realised rate
larger, because selected parents contribute unequally; @sec-cycles measures that
across cycles, and @sec-era-step4 shows how to read $\Delta F$ off a trajectory.
$N_e$ is a size defined by a rate, $N_e = 1/(2\Delta F)$ in @eq-hp-drift, and
so projects drift forward. The status number $N_s = 1/(2\theta_S)$ of @sec-ns has the
dimension of a count of individuals but is a static description of one set, and
does not project drift.

## Why the animal-breeding setting does not transfer directly {#sec-hp-not-animal}

Most theory for managing diversity under selection -- optimal contributions
[@meuwissen1997], the rate of inbreeding as the managed quantity, the comparison
of relationship matrices [@meuwissen2020] -- was developed for a randomly mating
population of non-inbred individuals in which the selection candidate is an
individual. A hybrid programme departs from that in three ways, each stated in the
preface and each made precise elsewhere:

1. **Parents are inbred.** Within-individual diversity of a parent is zero, so
   $GD_{WI} = 0$ exactly and individual $F$ is uninformative; the managed
   quantity is an allele frequency in a pool (@sec-subdivided, and A2 of
   @sec-era-programme).
2. **The population is permanently subdivided, and the subdivision is part of
   the product.** Between-pool divergence $GD_{BS}$ is to be maintained, not
   minimised as a symptom of drift; what it buys, and the conditions under which
   it buys nothing, are derived in @sec-heterosis.
3. **Candidates are crosses of fixed lines.** The coancestry of a set of single
   crosses is a quadratic form in how often each parent line is used, so the
   hybrid-by-hybrid matrix is never needed (@sec-collapse).

@sec-plant-literature sets these differences against what the applied plant
literature does, and @sec-era-transposition lists which assumptions of the
animal-breeding results fail in a hybrid crop.
